record.paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
record.original_question: How does noise influence rheological memory effects in soft glassy materials, particularly in experimentally accessible colloidal gels and soft glasses?

evidence.quote: Among the most pressing challenges stands the influence of noise on memory effect. Although researchers have explored and discussed its impact within the context of dense non-Brownian suspensions and 2D binary Lennard-Jones systems, 174,178 there remains a significant gap in experimental studies, particularly in the case of colloidal gels and soft glasses.

artifact.category_tag: rheological memory in soft glassy materials
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider soft amorphous materials such as colloidal gels and soft glasses, modeled as disordered systems that can encode "memory" of past mechanical training (for instance, the amplitude of prior oscillatory shear) and later reveal that memory through a read-out protocol (such as a strain sweep that exhibits a signature near the training amplitude). In such systems, thermal and/or athermal fluctuations ("noise") - arising from Brownian motion of constituents, microscopic plastic rearrangements, or external mechanical perturbations - compete with the encoding and retention of these rheological memories.

Problem. Develop a quantitative theory and accompanying experimental characterization of how noise of controlled type and intensity influences the encoding, storage, retrieval, and erasure of rheological memory effects in soft glassy materials, with explicit focus on experimentally accessible colloidal gels and soft glasses. Specifically:

(a) Formulate a model (e.g., a mesoscopic elastoplastic or trap-type model with an explicit noise term of tunable amplitude T) for an amorphous solid subjected to a memory-encoding shear protocol followed by a read-out protocol, and derive the dependence of the memory signal strength M on the noise amplitude T, the training amplitude γ_t, the waiting time t_w, and the read-out rate.

(b) Determine whether there exists a critical noise level T_c above which memory is destroyed, and characterize the scaling of M near T_c.

(c) Predict and experimentally verify, in colloidal gels and in soft glasses (e.g., concentrated emulsions, microgel pastes), how multiple memories can be simultaneously retained as a function of noise, including the maximum number of stable memories supported at a given T.

Provide either rigorous results, well-supported scaling laws, or experimentally validated phenomenology resolving these questions.
artifact.status_search_result: The influence of noise on memory effects has been studied in dense non-Brownian suspensions and in 2D binary Lennard-Jones simulations, but quantitative experimental and theoretical understanding for colloidal gels and soft glasses remains incomplete. Recent reviews on memory in matter (Keim et al.) and on yielding in amorphous solids continue to list noise-vs-memory in soft glassy systems as an open direction, with no comprehensive resolution found in the literature as of 2026.

status_evidence.title: Memory formation in matter (Rev. Mod. Phys.)
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews memory effects across disordered systems and highlights the role of noise; identifies open questions in soft glassy systems regarding how noise sets memory lifetimes.
status_evidence.claim: Noise effects on memory in soft glasses/colloidal gels remain an open area.

status_evidence.title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials
status_evidence.snippet: Identifies the influence of noise on memory effects in colloidal gels and soft glasses as a significant gap, particularly experimentally.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is highlighted as open and lacking experimental study.
